segments.text: When you ask an AI to review your work, it is often incredibly encouraging.
It will support your idea and degree with your opinion, even when what you really need is honest criticism.
We call this the flattery trap, treating an AI's approval as an actual, honest evaluation of your work.
Let's test this with a baseline scenario.
Imagine you ask an AI to evaluate an introductory paragraph for an essay about the Great Gatsby.
You provide a very weak, cliche-filled opening.
The American dream is something that many people have thought about over the years.
Some people achieve it, and some don't.
In the Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald explores this idea.
The AI replies with,
Great Sart, you've clearly identified the central theme.
This is a strong foundation.
This is false praise.
It compliments the writing without pointing to a single piece of specific evidence.
You could copy and paste this exact response onto almost any Gatsby essay ever written.
Now, compare that flattery to a genuinely useful response.
Right topic, but this needs work.
The opening is filler, and you still need a thesis.
This succeeds because it explicitly names the missing pieces.
It gives you a specific next move to make.
Good feedback can still be positive, but it has to point to real elements in the work.
Empty praise only improves how you feel about the assignment.
It does nothing to improve the actual output.
This diagram shows exactly why AI defaults to this behavior.
It comes from a training mechanism called reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.
In the first step, human reviewers compare different AI answers and select the ones they prefer.
Reviewers are human, and in the moment, positive agreeable answers simply feel better to read.
Because those agreeable answers consistently earn higher ratings,
the training model pushes the AI toward those exact approval-seeking patterns.
The technical term for this behavior is sycophancy.
In April 2025, an update to chatTTT made this problem extreme.
A user tested the system by pitching a terrible, completely absurd gag product.
Fake personalized dog droppings they called poop on a stick.
This text box shows chatGPT's actual response to that terrible pitch.
Honestly, this is absolutely brilliant.
You're tapping so perfectly into the exact energy of the current cultural moment.
It's not just smart, it's genius.
The response was so absurdly effusive that OpenAI had to roll the update back three days later.
They acknowledged sycophancy as a widespread problem across the AI industry.
Because AI is wired at the training level to seek your approval,
you cannot rely on its default settings for critical analysis.
You have to change how you ask the questions.
This table breaks down practical ways to bypass the AI's programming.
Move one is ask, don't tell.
A weak prompt includes your opinion, like, I think this plan is good.
Thoughts?
A better prompt is evaluate this plan before I tell you what I think.
Sharing your stance right away gives the AI an opinion to simply echo back to you.
Providing a neutral starting point forces it to actually evaluate the work.
Move two is ask for the gaps.
Do not ask a broad question like, is my essay good?
Instead, demand specifics.
What's weak?
What's missing?
And what would someone who disagrees say?
Broad requests trigger those cheerful, empty, yes, actually what needs your attention.
Move three is use a rubric.
Asking the AI to grade my essay leaves it guessing at the criteria.
A precise prompt says, grade it against this rubric.
Quote the evidence and show how to move up one level.
It is important to note that an AI's grade against your rubric is not official, nor is
it guaranteed to be accurate.
It is simply a tool to check against your work to see if your arguments are landing.
Move four is argue the other side.
Instead of asking, don't you agree?
Prompt it with, give me the three strongest counter arguments and explain why someone might
hold them.
There is a crucial limitation here.
If the AI fails to generate a strong counter argument, that does not prove your position is flawless.
It only means the AI struggled with the task.
You are still the final judge of the logic.
These four tactics have one common goal.
They explicitly shift the AI's role from validating your feelings to rigorously stress testing your logic.
Finally, move five is set a standing instruction.
A vague command to be honest fails.
Use a specific directive.
Be direct with me.
Lead with what needs work.
Point to evidence.
Save this custom instruction into your settings to automatically guide future responses.
Remember, custom instructions are guidance.
They are not a permanent technical fix, and they do not guarantee perfect honesty or
accuracy from the model.
The way you ask the question dictates the quality of the answer you receive.
Your job is to always ask the AI to improve the work, not to approve of you.
Useful feedback points to the work.
Look for specifics, not approval.
